headline: Strait of Hormuz Crisis Drives WTI Above $100 as Canada Posts 0.1% GDP Growth and 84,000 Job Losses
executive_summary:
The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since approximately March 2 — disrupting an estimated 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows, roughly 20% of global seaborne trade — drove WTI crude to US$102.88/bbl on March 30, the first settlement above $100 since July 2022.27 Brent crude surged approximately 55% in March to US$112.78/bbl, a record monthly gain for the contract since inception in 1988.27 The Dallas Federal Reserve estimated that a one-quarter closure could raise WTI to a $98/bbl average and reduce global GDP growth by an annualized 2.9 percentage points in Q2 2026.37 The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects and 785 power and energy projects across Canada, with Alberta accounting for 727 tracked projects that include upstream oil and gas operations.

Statistics Canada reported that employment declined by 84,000 (-0.4%) in February, reversing Q4 2025 gains.12 Full-time employment fell 108,000, private-sector employment dropped 73,000, and the unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January.12 Services-producing industries lost 56,000 positions and goods-producing industries lost 28,000, with wholesale and retail trade recording the largest subsector decline at 18,000 jobs.12 The database tracks 1,034 projects currently under construction that depend on labour market conditions.

Real GDP rose 0.1% in January 2026, marking a second consecutive monthly increase, according to Statistics Canada.4 Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction expanded 1.2%, while manufacturing contracted 1.4%.4 The advance estimate indicates 0.2% growth in February.4 Headline CPI fell to 1.8% year-over-year in February — the lowest since early 2021 — with core measures converging near 2.3-2.4%.8 The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18, citing weaker near-term growth from US tariffs and stating it would "proceed carefully" given heightened uncertainty.1

The merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December, as motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion — the lowest since September 2021.18 Energy exports partially offset the decline, rising 4.1%.18 The April 2 release of February trade data will be the first full month reflecting the Strait of Hormuz closure. On April 3, Statistics Canada releases the March Labour Force Survey, and on April 15, the Bank of Canada delivers its next rate decision alongside the full Monetary Policy Report and March CPI data.4243

national.analysis:
Statistics Canada reported real GDP grew 0.1% in January 2026, a second consecutive monthly increase following a flat December.4 Goods-producing industries expanded 0.2%, led by mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, which grew 1.2% in the month.4 Services-producing industries were essentially unchanged. Manufacturing contracted 1.4%, the steepest monthly decline in the current data cycle, reflecting weakness in both durable and non-durable goods production.4 Retail trade GDP rose 0.8%.4 The advance estimate for February indicates 0.2% growth.5 Q4 2025 GDP contracted 0.2% on an annualized basis, while full-year 2025 GDP growth was approximately 1.7%; the IMF projects 1.6% for 2026.67

The labour market recorded a contraction of 84,000 positions in February, the largest monthly decline since the pandemic recovery period.12 Full-time employment fell 108,000 while part-time employment rose 24,000. Private-sector employment dropped 73,000. The unemployment rate increased to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January, and the participation rate declined 0.1 percentage points to 64.9%.12 Services-producing industries shed 56,000 positions, with wholesale and retail trade losing 18,000 and other services declining 14,000. Goods-producing industries lost 28,000 positions.1213 Payroll employment from the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH) rose 45,600 (+0.2%) in January, providing a contrasting signal from the establishment survey.14

Headline CPI decelerated to 1.8% year-over-year in February 2026, down from 2.3% in January — the lowest reading since early 2021.8 All three Bank of Canada core measures converged: CPI-median at 2.3%, CPI-trim at 2.3%, and CPI-common at 2.4%.8 Food inflation slowed to 5.3% from 7.3% in January.910 The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18 — the seventh consecutive meeting at this level following seven cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.1 Bond markets priced approximately 86% probability of no change at the April 15 meeting.3

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December.18 Total exports fell 4.7% to $62.5 billion; imports declined 1.1% to $66.1 billion. Motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion, the lowest since September 2021, while energy product exports rose 4.1%.1819 Housing starts ran at 250,900 SAAR in February, up 4.5% from 240,148 in January, while the six-month trend declined 0.4% to 256,005 units.15 The average home price stood at $663,828 in February (+1.7% month-over-month).16 Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, with motor vehicle dealers leading at +2.0% and general merchandise retailers posting a fourth consecutive monthly increase at +3.0%.4041 Consumer confidence declined to 47.50 in February from 49.30 in January, while the Bloomberg/Nanos index showed a three-week slide into late March.3839

financialMarkets.summary:
The Bank of Canada's Governing Council held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18, maintaining its stance following seven consecutive cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.1 The Governing Council stated it would "proceed carefully" given heightened uncertainty from US tariffs. Bond markets priced approximately 86% probability of no change at the April 15 meeting, with 14% probability of a 25-basis-point increase.3 The Government of Canada 2-year yield stood at 2.95% and the 10-year at 3.58%, producing a 2-10 year spread of 0.63 percentage points. Year-over-year, the yield curve shifted upward across all terms: the 2-year rose from 2.62% and the 10-year from 3.22%.

WTI crude surged to US$102.88/bbl, up more than 50% in March — the first settlement above $100 since July 2022 — driven by the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupting approximately 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows.27 Brent crude settled at US$112.78/bbl, recording the largest monthly gain for the contract since inception in 1988.27 Natural gas (Henry Hub) traded at approximately US$3.05/MMBtu in late March; the EIA projects an average of $3.80 for 2026.2831 Gold declined approximately 14% in March to ~US$4,578/oz, the steepest monthly drop since October 2008, as margin liquidation and USD strength drove sellers.29 Copper traded in a range of US$5.25-$6.01/lb during March.30

The Canadian dollar weakened 1.85% month-over-month to 0.7198 CAD/USD (1.3893 USD/CAD), reflecting the 125-150 basis point spread between the Federal Reserve's 3.50-3.75% target and the BoC's 2.25%.24 The euro traded at 1.1460 EUR/USD, strengthening amid geopolitical uncertainty.25 The S&P/TSX Composite closed at 32,427 on March 31, up 1.54% on the day but down approximately 6% for March, while recording a 28.2% year-over-year gain.20 The S&P 500 closed at approximately 6,496, rallying 2.40% on March 31 — reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks contributed to the late-session advance — though the index remained approximately 9.4% below its January 2026 peak.2123

consumer_pulse:
The Conference Board of Canada's consumer confidence index declined to 47.50 in February from 49.30 in January.38 The Bloomberg/Nanos Canadian Confidence Index recorded a three-week slide into late March, with the index moving toward the neutral threshold.39 The proportion of Canadians expecting the economy to strengthen in six months rose from 17% to 26% over the four-week period, according to Nanos Research.39 Rising energy costs — with WTI above $100/bbl for the first time since 2022 — and US trade friction were the most frequently cited sources of consumer anxiety in sentiment tracking.

Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, according to Statistics Canada.40 Motor vehicle and parts dealers led the increase at +2.0%, while general merchandise retailers posted a fourth consecutive monthly gain at +3.0%.4041 Core retail sales (excluding gasoline stations and motor vehicle dealers) increased 0.9%. E-commerce sales rose 1.5% to $4.4 billion, representing 6.2% of total retail trade.40 Alberta recorded the largest provincial retail increase at +3.5%, led by motor vehicle sales.41 The advance estimate for February retail sales is +0.9%.40 Statistics Canada's CPI report showed food inflation decelerating to 5.3% from 7.3% in January, while headline inflation fell to 1.8% year-over-year — the lowest since early 2021.89

global.analysis:
The Federal Reserve held the federal funds target range at 3.50-3.75% at its March 18 meeting, following three 25-basis-point cuts in late 2025, citing "heightened uncertainty" from geopolitical risk and volatile energy prices.32 The US-Canada policy rate spread stands at 125-150 basis points, maintaining downward pressure on the Canadian dollar — CAD/USD weakened to 0.7198, a two-month low.24 US tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum exports remain in effect; the Bank of Canada attributed weaker Canadian near-term growth projections partly to these trade disruptions.1

US equity markets were dominated by Strait of Hormuz-related volatility in March. The S&P 500 stood at approximately 6,496 on March 31, down roughly 9.4% from its January 2026 peak.21 Reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks on March 31 triggered a broad rally: the S&P 500 gained 2.40%, the Nasdaq 3.24%, and the Dow approximately 2.0% on the session.23 Canada's merchandise trade with the US recorded a 21.2% decline in motor vehicle and parts exports to $5.4 billion in January — the lowest since September 2021 — directly linked to tariff-related disruptions.18

global.analysis:
China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.4 in March 2026, crossing above the 50.0 expansion threshold after two months of contraction (49.3 in January, 49.0 in February).35 The non-manufacturing PMI increased to 50.1 from 49.5, with new export orders showing strength.35 The People's Bank of China held the 5-year Loan Prime Rate at 2.90%. China recorded GDP growth of 5.0% for 2025, meeting the official annual target for a second consecutive year. CPI registered +0.2% year-over-year in February, reflecting subdued domestic demand.

China is Canada's second-largest merchandise trading partner, receiving approximately 5% of Canadian merchandise exports annually — crude oil, canola, potash, wood products, and seafood are the primary categories. The return to manufacturing expansion after two months of contraction could affect demand for these Canadian commodity exports through Q2 2026. Higher shipping costs from the Strait of Hormuz closure are affecting input prices for Chinese manufacturers and raising transport costs for Canadian LNG and commodity shipments routed to Asia.36 China controls an estimated 60% of global rare earth mine production and approximately 85% of downstream processing, a factor for Canadian critical minerals projects tracked in the database — the database contains 364 mining projects across Canada.

global.analysis:
The European Central Bank held its deposit facility rate at 2.00% at the March 19 meeting, maintaining its stance as euro area HICP inflation stood at 1.9% year-over-year in Q4 2025 — below the ECB's 2% target.3346 Euro area GDP grew 0.2% quarter-over-quarter in Q4 2025. Germany recorded a second consecutive annual GDP contraction, while Spain and Italy posted comparatively stronger output. Euro area unemployment stood at 5.9%.46

The ECB rate at 2.00% sits 25 basis points below the BoC's 2.25%, creating a narrow differential between the two central banks. The euro strengthened to 1.1460 EUR/USD on March 31 amid geopolitical uncertainty, which indirectly affects Canadian dollar competitiveness in European markets.25 Germany's continued contraction reduces demand for Canadian resource exports to Europe under the CETA (Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement) framework. The Strait of Hormuz closure has introduced energy supply and shipping cost pressures across the eurozone, which may alter trade flow patterns affecting Canadian commodity exporters.

The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its March 18 meeting by unanimous vote, maintaining its stance as UK CPI stood at 2.8% year-over-year in February 2026 — above the BoE's 2% target.34 UK GDP grew 0.1% quarter-over-quarter in Q4 2025, continuing a pattern of subdued output growth. Unemployment stood at 5.2%.47

The BoE rate at 3.75% exceeds the BoC's 2.25% by 150 basis points, reflecting persistent UK inflation relative to Canada's declining CPI trajectory. UK-Canada trade operates under the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) framework. GBP movements affect pricing for Canadian resource and agri-food exports to the UK. The Strait of Hormuz crisis has elevated energy import costs for the UK, which is a net energy importer, potentially affecting bilateral trade dynamics. The database tracks 7,372 total capital projects across Canada, with UK-linked investment flows most relevant to mining, energy, and financial services sectors.

watchlist.description: Detailed account of the Governing Council's March 18 rate decision deliberations, including assessment of US tariff impacts and inflation outlook. The summary will indicate the range of views on the policy rate path and whether any members favoured a different stance from the 2.25% hold.

Monthly export and import data. February is the first full month following the Strait of Hormuz closure initiation. Energy export values and automotive trade volumes are the key watch items. The database tracks 63 oil and gas projects and 600 transport and logistics projects.

First Q2 labour market reading. February recorded -84,000 employment change; March data will indicate whether the decline continued or reversed. The database tracks 1,034 projects under construction that depend on labour market conditions.

Monthly permit values by province and sector. A leading indicator for residential and non-residential construction activity. The database tracks 1,671 infrastructure projects and 211 residential projects.

Monthly CPI release. March is the final month affected by the GST/HST base-year effect. February headline CPI was 1.8%. Releases same day as the BoC rate decision — both data points together inform the policy rate path.
